## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Preprinted postcard sent by Nixon to supporters who had written after the speech
On the morning of September 24, Summerfield and Humphreys called Nixon at his Missoula hotel. After securing his agreement to fly to Wheeling if Eisenhower agreed to Chotiner's terms, the two reached Eisenhower and campaign leader New Hampshire Governor Sherman Adams in Portsmouth, Ohio, en route to Wheeling, and briefed them on the conversation with Nixon and on the flood of communications from the public. Eisenhower and Adams agreed that Nixon could come to Wheeling with the assurance he would remain on the ticket. After making speeches in Missoula and at a stop in Denver, and after Eisenhower made his own speech announcing that his running mate had been the victim of an "attempted smear," Nixon arrived in Wheeling late in the day on the 24th.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007258-72) Eisenhower came to the airport to meet the plane, and hurried up the steps to greet the Nixons when the door was opened.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTENixon1962123-73)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
The candidates waved at the crowd of 3,000 which had come to meet the plane, and rode together, with Nixon in place of honor, to a rally at City Island Stadium as Eisenhower chatted to Nixon as if the crisis had never occurred. At the stadium, Eisenhower introduced Nixon as a "colleague" who had been subject to "a vicious and unprincipled attack" but who had "vindicated himself" and who "stood higher than ever before".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007259-74) Eisenhower finished by reading two telegrams, one from Nixon's mother assuring Eisenhower of her son's integrity, and the second from Summerfield stating that the RNC had voted unanimously to retain Nixon on the ticket. Nixon then spoke, telling the crowd that this was one of two moments when he was most proud to be an American; the other had been at the victory parade in New York in 1945, when he had seen General Eisenhower go by. He called the Wheeling rally "the greatest moment of my life".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007259-74)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Editorial reaction to the address was divided. _The New York Times_, which had criticized Nixon, and had even run stories with claims that he was under criminal investigation for the Fund, praised Nixon's "composure and assurance".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990844-75)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990845-76) The _New York Journal-American_ gushed, "He was in our opinion, simply magnificent. We know of no other way to say it."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) The _Pittsburgh Press_ called the address "an extraordinary speech".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) The _Mobile Register_ stated that the Fund crisis "confronted [Nixon] with an unsought opportunity which he made the most of."[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMobile_Register8-78)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
However, some newspapers disagreed. _The Baltimore Sun_ noted that Nixon "did not deal in any way with the underlying question of propriety," while the _St. Louis Post-Dispatch_ called the address "a carefully contrived soap opera".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) Columnist Walter Lippmann called the wave of support for Nixon "disturbing... with all the magnification of modern electronics, simply mob law;"[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79) discussing the speech with a dinner guest, he said, "That must be the most demeaning experience my country has ever had to bear."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmbrose1988289-80) Columnist Thomas Stokes criticized Eisenhower for equivocating on the question of his running mate until "the young man himself—the accused—had to step in and take over. And how he took over!"[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79) Through his presidency, Eisenhower would continue to be accused of being indecisive.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Nixon refused to answer further questions about the Fund, and attention turned to Stevenson's fund, especially as its details became clear. Governor Stevenson's fund, which proved to total $146,000, had been used for such expenditures as Christmas gifts to reporters, dues for private clubs, and to hire an orchestra for a dance his son was hosting. Taking a leaf from Nixon's book, the Democrats refused to answer questions about Stevenson's fund. Both parties were eager to bury the matter, and the story died.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990851%E2%80%93852-81)
Wheeling Island Stadium (then City Island Stadium), site of the Republican rally on September 24, 1952

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
With _The New York Times_ finding that Nixon's performance had given the Republican ticket "a shot in the arm",[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990852-82) Eisenhower and Nixon swept to victory in November, with the Republicans narrowly taking both Houses of Congress.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990852-82) According to Nixon biographer Conrad Black, the speech earned Nixon supporters throughout Middle America which he would keep through the rest of his life, and who would continue to defend him after his death.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) Critics, however, would later see the address as the "ultimate expression" of the controversial politician's "phoniness".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenberg200431-84) Nixon biographer Stephen Ambrose stated that part of the audience considered the address "one of the most sickening, disgusting, maudlin performances ever experienced".[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmbrose1988289-80) In their analysis of the speech published just before Nixon's election as president in 1968, Robert S. Cathcart and Edward A. Schwarz suggested that while Nixon "met the accusation head-on and accomplished his immediate goals successfully, he ultimately created an image which led to a decline in his political career."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTECathcart_and_Schwarz9-85)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
The address was an unprecedented demonstration of the power of television to galvanize large segments of the American people to act in a political campaign.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKerbel199934-86) However, the onslaught of negative media attention leading up to the address "left its scars" on Nixon,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990855-87) and the future president never returned to the easy relationship with the press that he had enjoyed during his congressional career.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) His oft-stated view that the media was the enemy came to play a part in his downfall.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTESafire2008113%E2%80%93115-88)
The Nixons' black-and-white Cocker Spaniel Checkers (1952–1964)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Nixon celebrated the anniversary of the speech each year.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) The future president disliked the fact that the address soon became popularly known as the "Checkers speech". In his 1962 book, _Six Crises_ (the Fund crisis being one of the six), he would object to the term, "as though the mention of my dog was the only thing that saved my political career".[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTENixon1962125-89) Nixon preferred to call the address "the Fund speech,"[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHalberstam1993239%E2%80%93240-22) and made it required reading for his speechwriters.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTESafire2008113%E2%80%93115-88) As time passed, the Checkers speech became denigrated, and Nixon biographer Earl Mazo suggested that much of the attitude of "I don't like Nixon, but I don't know why," which contributed to the failure of his 1960 presidential run, can be traced to the Checkers speech.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBochin199044-90) Other commentators suggested that had he not made the Checkers speech, Nixon might have won in 1960. Nixon retorted that without the Checkers speech, he would not have been around to run in 1960.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBochin199044-90)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Checkers died in 1964 and was buried in Wantagh, New York, at Long Island's Bide-A-Wee Pet Cemetery.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''December_31,_1964-91) In 1999, 137 scholars of American public address were asked to recommend speeches for inclusion on a list of "the 100 best American political speeches of the 20th century," based on "social and political impact, and rhetorical artistry". This speech placed 6th on the list.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-92)
Despite the many criticisms of the speech in later years, Hal Bochin (who wrote a book about Nixon's rhetoric) suggests that Nixon succeeded at the time because of his use of narrative, spinning a story which resonated with the public:
> [The American people] could identify with the materials of the story—the low-cost apartment, the struggle with the mortgage payment, the parental loans, the lack of life insurance on the wife and children, and even the wife's cloth coat. By reputation, Nixon was a political fighter and also a family man, and the public admired the father who would not give back the family dog "regardless of what they said about it".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBochin199043-93)
"Checkers speech" has since entered the English lexicon as an idiom meaning a personal, emotionally-charged speech given by a politician in order to win support from the public.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDelahuntyDignen201279Safire2008113%E2%80%93115-94)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Preprinted postcard sent by Nixon to supporters who had written after the speech
On the morning of September 24, Summerfield and Humphreys called Nixon at his Missoula hotel. After securing his agreement to fly to Wheeling if Eisenhower agreed to Chotiner's terms, the two reached Eisenhower and campaign leader New Hampshire Governor Sherman Adams in Portsmouth, Ohio, en route to Wheeling, and briefed them on the conversation with Nixon and on the flood of communications from the public. Eisenhower and Adams agreed that Nixon could come to Wheeling with the assurance he would remain on the ticket. After making speeches in Missoula and at a stop in Denver, and after Eisenhower made his own speech announcing that his running mate had been the victim of an "attempted smear," Nixon arrived in Wheeling late in the day on the 24th.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007258-72) Eisenhower came to the airport to meet the plane, and hurried up the steps to greet the Nixons when the door was opened.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTENixon1962123-73)
texts.33:
## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
The candidates waved at the crowd of 3,000 which had come to meet the plane, and rode together, with Nixon in place of honor, to a rally at City Island Stadium as Eisenhower chatted to Nixon as if the crisis had never occurred. At the stadium, Eisenhower introduced Nixon as a "colleague" who had been subject to "a vicious and unprincipled attack" but who had "vindicated himself" and who "stood higher than ever before".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007259-74) Eisenhower finished by reading two telegrams, one from Nixon's mother assuring Eisenhower of her son's integrity, and the second from Summerfield stating that the RNC had voted unanimously to retain Nixon on the ticket. Nixon then spoke, telling the crowd that this was one of two moments when he was most proud to be an American; the other had been at the victory parade in New York in 1945, when he had seen General Eisenhower go by. He called the Wheeling rally "the greatest moment of my life".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007259-74)
texts.34:
## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Editorial reaction to the address was divided. _The New York Times_, which had criticized Nixon, and had even run stories with claims that he was under criminal investigation for the Fund, praised Nixon's "composure and assurance".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990844-75)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990845-76) The _New York Journal-American_ gushed, "He was in our opinion, simply magnificent. We know of no other way to say it."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) The _Pittsburgh Press_ called the address "an extraordinary speech".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) The _Mobile Register_ stated that the Fund crisis "confronted [Nixon] with an unsought opportunity which he made the most of."[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMobile_Register8-78)
texts.35:
## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
However, some newspapers disagreed. _The Baltimore Sun_ noted that Nixon "did not deal in any way with the underlying question of propriety," while the _St. Louis Post-Dispatch_ called the address "a carefully contrived soap opera".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) Columnist Walter Lippmann called the wave of support for Nixon "disturbing... with all the magnification of modern electronics, simply mob law;"[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79) discussing the speech with a dinner guest, he said, "That must be the most demeaning experience my country has ever had to bear."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmbrose1988289-80) Columnist Thomas Stokes criticized Eisenhower for equivocating on the question of his running mate until "the young man himself—the accused—had to step in and take over. And how he took over!"[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79) Through his presidency, Eisenhower would continue to be accused of being indecisive.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79)
texts.36:
## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Nixon refused to answer further questions about the Fund, and attention turned to Stevenson's fund, especially as its details became clear. Governor Stevenson's fund, which proved to total $146,000, had been used for such expenditures as Christmas gifts to reporters, dues for private clubs, and to hire an orchestra for a dance his son was hosting. Taking a leaf from Nixon's book, the Democrats refused to answer questions about Stevenson's fund. Both parties were eager to bury the matter, and the story died.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990851%E2%80%93852-81)

texts.37:
## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
With _The New York Times_ finding that Nixon's performance had given the Republican ticket "a shot in the arm",[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990852-82) Eisenhower and Nixon swept to victory in November, with the Republicans narrowly taking both Houses of Congress.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990852-82) According to Nixon biographer Conrad Black, the speech earned Nixon supporters throughout Middle America which he would keep through the rest of his life, and who would continue to defend him after his death.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) Critics, however, would later see the address as the "ultimate expression" of the controversial politician's "phoniness".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenberg200431-84) Nixon biographer Stephen Ambrose stated that part of the audience considered the address "one of the most sickening, disgusting, maudlin performances ever experienced".[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmbrose1988289-80) In their analysis of the speech published just before Nixon's election as president in 1968, Robert S. Cathcart and Edward A. Schwarz suggested that while Nixon "met the accusation head-on and accomplished his immediate goals successfully, he ultimately created an image which led to a decline in his political career."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTECathcart_and_Schwarz9-85)
texts.38:
## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
The address was an unprecedented demonstration of the power of television to galvanize large segments of the American people to act in a political campaign.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKerbel199934-86) However, the onslaught of negative media attention leading up to the address "left its scars" on Nixon,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990855-87) and the future president never returned to the easy relationship with the press that he had enjoyed during his congressional career.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) His oft-stated view that the media was the enemy came to play a part in his downfall.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTESafire2008113%E2%80%93115-88)
The Nixons' black-and-white Cocker Spaniel Checkers (1952–1964)
texts.39:
## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Nixon celebrated the anniversary of the speech each year.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) The future president disliked the fact that the address soon became popularly known as the "Checkers speech". In his 1962 book, _Six Crises_ (the Fund crisis being one of the six), he would object to the term, "as though the mention of my dog was the only thing that saved my political career".[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTENixon1962125-89) Nixon preferred to call the address "the Fund speech,"[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHalberstam1993239%E2%80%93240-22) and made it required reading for his speechwriters.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTESafire2008113%E2%80%93115-88) As time passed, the Checkers speech became denigrated, and Nixon biographer Earl Mazo suggested that much of the attitude of "I don't like Nixon, but I don't know why," which contributed to the failure of his 1960 presidential run, can be traced to the Checkers speech.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBochin199044-90) Other commentators suggested that had he not made the Checkers speech, Nixon might have won in 1960. Nixon retorted that without the Checkers speech, he would not have been around to run in 1960.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBochin199044-90)
texts.40:
## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Checkers died in 1964 and was buried in Wantagh, New York, at Long Island's Bide-A-Wee Pet Cemetery.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''December_31,_1964-91) In 1999, 137 scholars of American public address were asked to recommend speeches for inclusion on a list of "the 100 best American political speeches of the 20th century," based on "social and political impact, and rhetorical artistry". This speech placed 6th on the list.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-92)
Despite the many criticisms of the speech in later years, Hal Bochin (who wrote a book about Nixon's rhetoric) suggests that Nixon succeeded at the time because of his use of narrative, spinning a story which resonated with the public:
> [The American people] could identify with the materials of the story—the low-cost apartment, the struggle with the mortgage payment, the parental loans, the lack of life insurance on the wife and children, and even the wife's cloth coat. By reputation, Nixon was a political fighter and also a family man, and the public admired the father who would not give back the family dog "regardless of what they said about it".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBochin199043-93)
"Checkers speech" has since entered the English lexicon as an idiom meaning a personal, emotionally-charged speech given by a politician in order to win support from the public.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDelahuntyDignen201279Safire2008113%E2%80%93115-94)

On the morning of September 24, Summerfield and Humphreys called Nixon at his Missoula hotel. After securing his agreement to fly to Wheeling if Eisenhower agreed to Chotiner's terms, the two reached Eisenhower and campaign leader New Hampshire Governor Sherman Adams in Portsmouth, Ohio, en route to Wheeling, and briefed them on the conversation with Nixon and on the flood of communications from the public. Eisenhower and Adams agreed that Nixon could come to Wheeling with the assurance he would remain on the ticket. After making speeches in Missoula and at a stop in Denver, and after Eisenhower made his own speech announcing that his running mate had been the victim of an "attempted smear," Nixon arrived in Wheeling late in the day on the 24th.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007258-72) Eisenhower came to the airport to meet the plane, and hurried up the steps to greet the Nixons when the door was opened.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTENixon1962123-73)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
The candidates waved at the crowd of 3,000 which had come to meet the plane, and rode together, with Nixon in place of honor, to a rally at City Island Stadium as Eisenhower chatted to Nixon as if the crisis had never occurred. At the stadium, Eisenhower introduced Nixon as a "colleague" who had been subject to "a vicious and unprincipled attack" but who had "vindicated himself" and who "stood higher than ever before".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007259-74) Eisenhower finished by reading two telegrams, one from Nixon's mother assuring Eisenhower of her son's integrity, and the second from Summerfield stating that the RNC had voted unanimously to retain Nixon on the ticket. Nixon then spoke, telling the crowd that this was one of two moments when he was most proud to be an American; the other had been at the victory parade in New York in 1945, when he had seen General Eisenhower go by. He called the Wheeling rally "the greatest moment of my life".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007259-74)

## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
Editorial reaction to the address was divided. _The New York Times_, which had criticized Nixon, and had even run stories with claims that he was under criminal investigation for the Fund, praised Nixon's "composure and assurance".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990844-75)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990845-76) The _New York Journal-American_ gushed, "He was in our opinion, simply magnificent. We know of no other way to say it."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) The _Pittsburgh Press_ called the address "an extraordinary speech".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) The _Mobile Register_ stated that the Fund crisis "confronted [Nixon] with an unsought opportunity which he made the most of."[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMobile_Register8-78)

However, some newspapers disagreed. _The Baltimore Sun_ noted that Nixon "did not deal in any way with the underlying question of propriety," while the _St. Louis Post-Dispatch_ called the address "a carefully contrived soap opera".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_Washington_Post''September_25,_1952-77) Columnist Walter Lippmann called the wave of support for Nixon "disturbing... with all the magnification of modern electronics, simply mob law;"[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79) discussing the speech with a dinner guest, he said, "That must be the most demeaning experience my country has ever had to bear."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmbrose1988289-80) Columnist Thomas Stokes criticized Eisenhower for equivocating on the question of his running mate until "the young man himself—the accused—had to step in and take over. And how he took over!"[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79) Through his presidency, Eisenhower would continue to be accused of being indecisive.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990854-79)

Nixon refused to answer further questions about the Fund, and attention turned to Stevenson's fund, especially as its details became clear. Governor Stevenson's fund, which proved to total $146,000, had been used for such expenditures as Christmas gifts to reporters, dues for private clubs, and to hire an orchestra for a dance his son was hosting. ## Delivering the address
### Candidates and public
With _The New York Times_ finding that Nixon's performance had given the Republican ticket "a shot in the arm",[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990852-82) Eisenhower and Nixon swept to victory in November, with the Republicans narrowly taking both Houses of Congress.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990852-82) According to Nixon biographer Conrad Black, the speech earned Nixon supporters throughout Middle America which he would keep through the rest of his life, and who would continue to defend him after his death.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) Critics, however, would later see the address as the "ultimate expression" of the controversial politician's "phoniness".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenberg200431-84) Nixon biographer Stephen Ambrose stated that part of the audience considered the address "one of the most sickening, disgusting, maudlin performances ever experienced".[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmbrose1988289-80) In their analysis of the speech published just before Nixon's election as president in 1968, Robert S. Cathcart and Edward A. Schwarz suggested that while Nixon "met the accusation head-on and accomplished his immediate goals successfully, he ultimately created an image which led to a decline in his political career."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTECathcart_and_Schwarz9-85)

The address was an unprecedented demonstration of the power of television to galvanize large segments of the American people to act in a political campaign.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKerbel199934-86) However, the onslaught of negative media attention leading up to the address "left its scars" on Nixon,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorris1990855-87) and the future president never returned to the easy relationship with the press that he had enjoyed during his congressional career.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) His oft-stated view that the media was the enemy came to play a part in his downfall.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTESafire2008113%E2%80%93115-88)

Nixon celebrated the anniversary of the speech each year.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlack2007261-83) The future president disliked the fact that the address soon became popularly known as the "Checkers speech". In his 1962 book, _Six Crises_ (the Fund crisis being one of the six), he would object to the term, "as though the mention of my dog was the only thing that saved my political career".[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTENixon1962125-89) Nixon preferred to call the address "the Fund speech,"[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHalberstam1993239%E2%80%93240-22) and made it required reading for his speechwriters.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTESafire2008113%E2%80%93115-88) As time passed, the Checkers speech became denigrated, and Nixon biographer Earl Mazo suggested that much of the attitude of "I don't like Nixon, but I don't know why," which contributed to the failure of his 1960 presidential run, can be traced to the Checkers speech.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBochin199044-90) Other commentators suggested that had he not made the Checkers speech, Nixon might have won in 1960. Nixon retorted that without the Checkers speech, he would not have been around to run in 1960.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBochin199044-90)

Checkers died in 1964 and was buried in Wantagh, New York, at Long Island's Bide-A-Wee Pet Cemetery.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkers_speech#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''December_31,_1964-91) In 1999, 137 scholars of American public address were asked to recommend speeches for inclusion on a list of "the 100 best American political speeches of the 20th century," based on "social and political impact, and rhetorical artistry". ### Richard Nixon
(January 9, 1913 - April 22, 1994)
Richard Milhous Nixon was born on January 9, 1913 on the lemon ranch of his parents, Francis and Hannah Nixon in Yorba Linda, California and raised in nearby Whittier. He attended Whittier College and Duke University School of Law and then joined a law firm in his hometown. He and Patricia "Pat" Ryan met in 1938 at rehearsal for a community play in which they were both acting. They were married in 1940, and would later have two daughters, Patricia (Tricia) (1946) and Julie (1948). In 1942 he received a Navy commission and served in the Pacific theatre.
Nixon won a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in 1946. In 1948, as a member of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), he led the investigation of Alger Hiss, a former State Department official accused of spying for the Soviet Union. After two terms he was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1950.
In 1952, General Dwight D. Eisenhower selected Nixon as his running mate. Two months later, an article was published claiming that campaign donors were buying influence with Nixon. To rebut his critics, Nixon appeared on television to the largest audience in history to date. In the live, nationwide broadcast, Nixon said that his family had accepted one campaign gift for themselves: a beloved dog named Checkers whom they intended to keep. The speech was a great success, proving the importance of television as a political medium.
The Eisenhower-Nixon ticket won the 1952 Presidential election and was re-elected to a second term in 1956. Vice President Nixon undertook many goodwill tours of foreign countries in an effort to increase support for American policies during the Cold War. After losing the 1960 Presidential election to John F. Kennedy and an unsuccessful bid for governor of California in 1962, he practiced law, wrote, and traveled extensively in Europe and Asia.

### Richard Nixon
In 1968 Nixon was elected the 37th President of the U.S. Nixon’s foreign policy aimed to reduce international tensions by forging new links with old rivals. He began normalizing diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China, established the policy of détente with the Soviet Union and pursued domestic initiatives that included establishing the Environmental Protection Agency and bringing about the peaceful desegregation of public schools in the South.
On July 20, 1969, Nixon made what has been termed the longest-distance telephone call ever when he spoke from the Oval Office to astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin during man’s first landing on the moon.
Following Vice President Spiro Agnew's resignation in October 1973, Nixon nominated House Minority Leader Gerald R. Ford to succeed Agnew. Following revelations from the Watergate tapes, Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974. Vice President Ford then became president of the United States.
In retirement, Nixon traveled throughout the United States and dozens of countries in Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Mideast. In addition to his travels, Nixon kept up a full schedule of speaking and writing, completing ten books during his post-presidential lifetime. Nixon died on April 22, 1994, in New York City and was buried in Yorba Linda, California on April 27, 1994.

### Richard Nixon
(January 9, 1913 - April 22, 1994)
Richard Milhous Nixon was born on January 9, 1913 on the lemon ranch of his parents, Francis and Hannah Nixon in Yorba Linda, California and raised in nearby Whittier. He attended Whittier College and Duke University School of Law and then joined a law firm in his hometown. He and Patricia "Pat" Ryan met in 1938 at rehearsal for a community play in which they were both acting. They were married in 1940, and would later have two daughters, Patricia (Tricia) (1946) and Julie (1948). In 1942 he received a Navy commission and served in the Pacific theatre.
Nixon won a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in 1946. In 1948, as a member of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), he led the investigation of Alger Hiss, a former State Department official accused of spying for the Soviet Union. After two terms he was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1950.
In 1952, General Dwight D. Eisenhower selected Nixon as his running mate. Two months later, an article was published claiming that campaign donors were buying influence with Nixon. To rebut his critics, Nixon appeared on television to the largest audience in history to date. In the live, nationwide broadcast, Nixon said that his family had accepted one campaign gift for themselves: a beloved dog named Checkers whom they intended to keep. The speech was a great success, proving the importance of television as a political medium.
The Eisenhower-Nixon ticket won the 1952 Presidential election and was re-elected to a second term in 1956. Vice President Nixon undertook many goodwill tours of foreign countries in an effort to increase support for American policies during the Cold War. After losing the 1960 Presidential election to John F. Kennedy and an unsuccessful bid for governor of California in 1962, he practiced law, wrote, and traveled extensively in Europe and Asia.

### Richard Nixon
In 1968 Nixon was elected the 37th President of the U.S. Nixon’s foreign policy aimed to reduce international tensions by forging new links with old rivals. He began normalizing diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China, established the policy of détente with the Soviet Union and pursued domestic initiatives that included establishing the Environmental Protection Agency and bringing about the peaceful desegregation of public schools in the South.
On July 20, 1969, Nixon made what has been termed the longest-distance telephone call ever when he spoke from the Oval Office to astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin during man’s first landing on the moon.
Following Vice President Spiro Agnew's resignation in October 1973, Nixon nominated House Minority Leader Gerald R. Ford to succeed Agnew. Following revelations from the Watergate tapes, Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974. Vice President Ford then became president of the United States.
In retirement, Nixon traveled throughout the United States and dozens of countries in Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Mideast. In addition to his travels, Nixon kept up a full schedule of speaking and writing, completing ten books during his post-presidential lifetime. Nixon died on April 22, 1994, in New York City and was buried in Yorba Linda, California on April 27, 1994.
